Family Health

Colon cancer: diagnosis, treatment and the next steps

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Finding colon cancer early can make a difference, but screening, confirming a diagnosis and choosing treatment are separate steps. This guide explains the tests and treatment options, the questions worth asking and the limits of general statistics when decisions are about one person.

Screening and investigating symptoms are different

Colon cancer may cause no symptoms at first. Screening looks for cancer or precancerous changes in people who feel well; diagnostic tests investigate symptoms or an abnormal screening result. Removing some polyps can prevent a cancer from developing. A positive screening test is a reason for follow-up, not a diagnosis by itself.

In the United States, average-risk screening generally begins at 45. Other countries use different programmes, and family history, previous polyps or certain bowel and inherited conditions may require an earlier or different plan. Symptoms need assessment at any age. Do not wait to reach a screening age if you have persistent unexplained bowel changes or bleeding.

The first appointment: history and examination

The clinician may ask about bowel habits, blood in the stool, abdominal discomfort, weight changes, fatigue and how long symptoms have lasted. Bring details of previous tests and any relatives with colorectal cancer or significant polyps, including their ages at diagnosis. Medicines and other bowel conditions also help guide the investigation.

An abdominal examination and, when appropriate, a rectal examination can identify some abnormalities. A normal examination cannot rule out a cancer farther up the colon. Ask which test comes next, how quickly it should happen and what to do if symptoms worsen while you are waiting.

Guaiac stool testing: gFOBT

A guaiac-based faecal occult blood test uses a chemical reaction to look for hidden blood in stool. It may require samples from several bowel movements. Some foods and medicines can interfere with the result, so follow the exact kit instructions rather than advice intended for a different stool test.

Do not stop prescribed aspirin, blood thinners or another essential medicine without the prescriber’s advice. A stool sample obtained during a single office rectal examination is not an adequate substitute for a recommended screening programme. Blood detected by gFOBT can have causes other than colorectal cancer.

FIT: a different way to look for hidden blood

The faecal immunochemical test, or FIT, uses antibodies to detect human haemoglobin. It is more focused on bleeding from the lower digestive tract than gFOBT and generally does not require dietary restrictions. Many kits use a small sample from one bowel movement, but collection requirements depend on the kit and programme.

An abnormal screening FIT normally needs colonoscopy to find the cause. Repeating FIT to obtain a reassuring result does not complete that follow-up. A negative result also cannot explain away persistent symptoms: discuss ongoing bleeding, bowel changes or unexplained anaemia with the clinician who arranged the test.

What a home kit does (and does not) provide

Home collection is a convenient way to provide a sample, not a diagnosis of every bowel disorder. Some stool tests combine blood detection with DNA or RNA markers. These have their own eligibility criteria and intervals. A product being sold online does not establish that it is the right test for your symptoms or risk.

Check the collection, storage and return instructions and make a note of when results are expected. There is no universal five-day turnaround or instant home-test diagnosis of cancer or colitis. If a sample is inadequate, ask how to repeat it correctly; if a screening result is abnormal, complete the recommended investigation.

Colonoscopy can examine, sample and remove

Colonoscopy uses a flexible instrument to examine the rectum and the full colon. It can be used as the initial screening test, to investigate symptoms or after another test is abnormal. The clinician can remove suitable polyps and take tissue samples for a pathologist to examine.

Preparation usually includes clearing the bowel, and comfort or sedation options should be discussed beforehand. For a normal, high-quality examination in an average-risk US screening programme, the interval is commonly ten years, not every year. Findings, incomplete preparation, family history or symptoms can change that interval. Follow the report’s individual recommendation.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines the lower bowel

Sigmoidoscopy uses a shorter instrument and examines the rectum and lower part of the colon. It does not inspect the entire colon. An abnormality may lead to a full colonoscopy, and a normal result does not exclude a problem beyond the area reached.

As an example, US screening options include sigmoidoscopy every five years, or every ten years when combined with annual FIT. These are programme options for appropriate people, not instructions for everyone with symptoms. Availability and local recommendations differ, so ask why this examination has been chosen for you.

CT colonography and the older barium enema

CT colonography uses a dedicated CT technique to create views of the colon. It usually requires bowel preparation and cannot remove a polyp or take a biopsy. An abnormal finding may therefore need colonoscopy. In US average-risk screening it is commonly repeated every five years. It is different from an ordinary abdominal CT used to assess cancer spread.

A double-contrast barium enema outlines the bowel with contrast material for X-ray images. Barium itself is not radioactive; the imaging uses X-rays. This is now rarely used for colorectal screening and should not be presented as the routine modern alternative to colonoscopy. The appropriate imaging test depends on the clinical question.

Blood tests and biopsy answer different questions

A blood count can show anaemia, and other blood tests may assess liver function or overall health. These findings help guide care but cannot on their own confirm or exclude colorectal cancer. CEA, a tumour marker sometimes used during follow-up, is not a stand-alone screening or diagnostic test.

A diagnosis generally depends on examination of tissue from a biopsy or removed lesion. Some results may be available promptly, while pathology can take longer. Ask when and how you will hear the result. If cancer is found, additional imaging and tests help define its extent and guide treatment.

Stage, location and tumour biology guide treatment

The cancer team considers how deeply the tumour has grown, whether lymph nodes are involved and whether it has spread to distant sites. Stage 0 describes disease confined to the innermost lining; stages I to III describe increasing local or regional involvement, and stage IV involves distant spread.

The exact location, whether surgery is feasible, your health and the tumour’s molecular features also matter. Colon and rectal cancers are related but do not always receive the same treatment. Ask about mismatch-repair or microsatellite-instability results and any other biomarkers relevant to treatment or possible inherited risk.

Surgery for a polyp or a cancer in the colon

Some very early cancers within a polyp can be treated during colonoscopy. Whether that is sufficient depends on the depth, completeness of removal, tissue margins and other pathological features. It is not enough simply to describe the growth as small or “not attached” to the bowel wall.

For many localized colon cancers, surgery removes the affected segment and nearby lymph nodes. The surgeon may reconnect the healthy ends of the bowel. The operation may be performed through smaller incisions or an open approach, depending on the situation. Lymph-node examination helps determine whether further treatment is needed.

When a stoma or another operation may be needed

Sometimes the bowel cannot safely be reconnected immediately. A colostomy or ileostomy brings bowel to an opening in the abdominal skin so waste can collect in a pouch. A stoma may be temporary or permanent; it is not inevitable for every person with colon cancer.

A specialist stoma nurse can explain pouch care and practical adjustments. In advanced disease, an operation or stent may relieve an obstruction. Selected people with limited spread, for example to the liver or lungs, may also be considered for treatment directed at those sites. Ask whether each procedure aims to cure the cancer, control it or relieve symptoms.

Chemotherapy before or after surgery

Chemotherapy is commonly offered after surgery for stage III colon cancer and may be considered for selected higher-risk stage II cancers. Some locally advanced or metastatic cancers receive drug treatment before an operation or as the main way to control disease. The timing and expected benefit should be explained for your own case.

Medicines include fluorouracil, often called 5-FU, capecitabine, oxaliplatin and irinotecan, used in particular combinations and settings. Not every person needs every drug. Regimens, doses and duration depend on the purpose of treatment, other health conditions and how well it is tolerated. Oral chemotherapy also requires careful instructions and monitoring.

Radiotherapy has a more selective role in colon cancer

Radiotherapy is more commonly part of rectal-cancer treatment than routine colon-cancer treatment. For colon cancer, it may be considered in selected local situations or to relieve symptoms such as pain, bleeding or problems from disease at other sites. It may sometimes be combined with chemotherapy.

Ask which area will be treated, the goal and likely short- and longer-term effects. Bowel irritation, fatigue, skin changes and effects on nearby organs depend on the field and dose. A treatment described for rectal cancer should not automatically be assumed to be the standard plan for a colon tumour.

Targeted drugs: the tumour’s features matter

Targeted medicines interfere with particular growth pathways. Bevacizumab, ramucirumab and ziv-aflibercept affect blood-vessel signalling. Cetuximab and panitumumab act on EGFR; their use depends on molecular results and treatment context, often including RAS status. Regorafenib blocks several kinases and is one option in selected later treatment settings.

Other targeted combinations may be relevant to specific changes such as BRAF, HER2 or KRAS alterations. This is a rapidly changing field, and a list of drug names cannot replace tumour testing and specialist selection. The medicines have different side effects and are not equally suitable or approved in every country.

Immunotherapy is a separate treatment category

Pembrolizumab and nivolumab are checkpoint inhibitors that help the immune system act against cancer. Ipilimumab may be used with nivolumab in an appropriate regimen. Their colorectal-cancer use is strongly linked to features such as high microsatellite instability, or MSI-H, and deficient mismatch repair, or dMMR. They are not interchangeable with every targeted drug.

Immunotherapy is not necessarily a last-resort treatment. For example, the FDA approved nivolumab with ipilimumab in April 2025 for unresectable or metastatic MSI-H/dMMR colorectal cancer without requiring prior chemotherapy. This US indication does not establish local availability or suitability for everyone. Earlier-stage uses also require a specialist plan rather than extrapolation from metastatic treatment.

Plan for side effects and follow-up

Drug treatment can cause fatigue, mouth or bowel symptoms and changes in blood counts. Certain medicines can cause nerve symptoms or sensitivity to cold, while immunotherapy can trigger inflammation in otherwise healthy organs. Tell the team about new symptoms promptly instead of assuming all side effects are unavoidable.

Keep the oncology contact number and follow its instructions for fever, infection symptoms, severe diarrhoea, dehydration or breathing problems. The team can often adjust supportive care or treatment. Follow-up after treatment may include examinations, blood tests, imaging and colonoscopy at an individualized schedule; feeling well does not remove the need for that plan.

Understanding survival figures without treating them as a forecast

The US NCI SEER figures checked for this review report five-year relative survival for colorectal cancer diagnosed in 2016–2022: 91.3% for localized disease, 75.2% for regional disease and 16.9% for distant disease; the overall figure is 65.4%. These are combined colon-and-rectum statistics, not colon-only estimates.

The SEER groups do not map exactly onto numbered stages I, II, III and IV. Relative survival compares outcomes with those expected without the cancer; five years is a measurement interval, not a personal deadline. These population figures cannot predict an individual outcome, and newer treatments may not be fully reflected. Your team can explain the factors most relevant to you.

Reducing risk: screening and everyday choices

No habit guarantees prevention, but appropriate screening, avoiding tobacco, regular physical activity and a healthy weight can reduce risk. A dietary pattern with vegetables, fruit, whole grains and other fibre-containing foods, while limiting red and processed meats, is more useful than a blanket instruction to eliminate all dietary fat.

Avoiding alcohol is the lowest-risk option for cancer prevention. If you drink, reducing intake can help. Managing diabetes supports overall health, but does not remove colorectal-cancer risk or the need for screening. Family history and other factors outside your control still matter; developing cancer is not proof that someone failed to live correctly.

Nutrition and emotional support during treatment

Prevention advice is not a prescription for weight loss during cancer treatment. Eating difficulties, bowel surgery, a stoma or unwanted weight loss may require a different diet and help from a cancer dietitian. Tell the team about supplements and major dietary changes before starting them.

Fear, sadness and uncertainty are understandable. Counselling, support groups and practical help can make treatment more manageable. Stress reduction is useful for wellbeing, but it is not a proven way to prevent or cure colon cancer. Spiritual support can be included if it matters to you; nobody needs to maintain a particular attitude to deserve care.

Make the next step specific

Before leaving an appointment, ask what is known, which result is still pending and who will contact you. After diagnosis, request an explanation of the stage, biomarker findings, treatment goal and alternatives. Bring a support person if helpful and write down questions as they arise.

Seek prompt assessment for persistent unexplained bleeding or bowel changes. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting or inability to pass stool or gas, heavy bleeding or fainting needs urgent care. During treatment, use the oncology team’s urgent instructions. A clear contact and follow-up plan helps avoid both missed results and uncertainty about when to call.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC, NCI, NHS and ACS guidance distinguishes screening intervals from diagnostic assessment. The numerical screening intervals here are US examples for eligible average-risk adults, not a universal schedule or a substitute for investigating symptoms.

ACS and NCI describe stage- and biomarker-directed treatment. The FDA’s April 2025 nivolumab/ipilimumab indication updates older last-line-only wording. SEER survival figures are US combined colorectal data for 2016–2022, with summary-stage groups kept distinct from numbered cancer stages.

How BeMama can help

Keep a single record of test dates, results and the next appointment. Ask the team to explain the purpose of each test or treatment and who to call if a result or symptom needs follow-up.

When to seek help

A negative home test does not explain persistent symptoms. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting or inability to pass stool or gas, heavy bleeding or fainting needs urgent care. During cancer treatment, follow the team’s urgent symptom instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An abnormal screening test needs follow-up; it is not a diagnosis on its own.
  • Colonoscopy can examine the whole colon and obtain tissue.
  • Treatment depends on stage, tumour biology, health and personal priorities.
  • Radiotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy have distinct roles.
  • Population survival figures cannot predict one person’s outcome.

Frequently asked questions

Does a positive FIT mean I have cancer?

No. It detects blood, which can have several causes. An abnormal screening result usually needs colonoscopy to investigate the reason.

Can I repeat FIT instead of attending colonoscopy?

A later negative test does not complete the follow-up of an abnormal screening FIT. Discuss the recommended investigation with your clinician.

Do I need colonoscopy every year from age 40?

Not as a general rule. Age and intervals depend on risk and local guidance. A normal high-quality US average-risk screening colonoscopy is commonly followed at ten years; symptoms or findings can change the plan.

Can a blood count or CEA diagnose colon cancer?

No. These can contribute to assessment or monitoring, but neither confirms or excludes the diagnosis on its own.

Is the barium used in a barium enema radioactive?

No. Barium is a contrast material that helps outline the bowel on X-ray images. The test is now rarely used for colorectal screening.

Will colon surgery always mean a permanent bag?

No. A stoma may be unnecessary, temporary or permanent, depending on the operation and circumstances. Ask the surgeon what is likely in your case.

Does everyone with colon cancer need radiotherapy?

No. It is more commonly used for rectal cancer and has selected roles in colon cancer. Ask about the specific aim if it is recommended.

Are pembrolizumab, nivolumab and ipilimumab ordinary targeted drugs?

They are immune checkpoint treatments. The appropriate regimen depends on biomarkers and clinical context; ipilimumab is used with nivolumab in relevant colorectal regimens.

Does a five-year survival percentage tell me how long I will live?

No. It describes a population over a defined interval. Individual prognosis depends on many factors, and the statistics are not a deadline.

Can reducing stress prevent or cure colon cancer?

Stress support can improve wellbeing, but it is not established as a way to prevent or cure the disease. Screening and evidence-based care remain important.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
